data: The goal is to classify photographs of moving fabric as defective or defect_free. The images are 2448×2048 RGB frames from a fixed camera over three fabrics (blue, lilac, mauve), captured about one second apart. 5,025 frames were sorted into Defected, Defect Free and Wasted using the course procedure. Wasted frames (creases with no defect, the instructor's hand, fabric joints; 98 images) are excluded because the task has two classes. 26 byte-identical duplicates were also removed, so a test image cannot be an exact copy of a training image. That leaves 4,901 images: 3,490 defective (71%) and 1,411 defect_free (29%). One labelling rule mattered: any white mark that stands out from the fabric counts as a defect, even when the fabric is also creased, and dark spots (dust on the lens) do not.
split: The 70/20/10 split was made once, in Roboflow, and exported as-is to train the CNN, so both models see exactly the same train, validation and test images. The 50 images for infer.py were drawn at random (stratified by class, fixed seed) from the test split, which neither model trains on.
pipelines: Both pipelines use transfer learning from ImageNet weights, which is the realistic choice for 3,431 training images. The main design difference is resolution. Roboflow's classifier works at 224×224. For the CNN we kept 512×512, because many defects are a few pixels wide in the original frame and disappear when it is shrunk tenfold. Class imbalance (71/29) is handled in the CNN with an inverse-frequency weighted loss; Roboflow has no equivalent setting.
